subject: Cloud Computing
title: The Shared Responsibility Model
description: A fast breakdown of The Shared Responsibility Model for builders.

hook.text: When your cloud app gets hacked, whose fault is it? The answer depends on which service model you use.

buildup.text: Cloud providers and customers split responsibility. The provider secures the infrastructure below you.

discovery.text: With IaaS, you secure the OS, apps, and data. With SaaS, the provider handles almost everything.

twist.text: Most cloud breaches happen because customers misconfigure their part — not because the provider failed.

climax.text: Understanding where your responsibility starts is the first step to real cloud security.

punchline.text: The cloud is secure. Your configuration might not be.

quiz.question: What causes most cloud security breaches?
options: Customer misconfiguration, not cloud provider failures
Hackers breaking through cloud provider firewalls

details.summary: The shared responsibility model defines which security tasks belong to the cloud provider and which belong to the customer. Responsibility shifts with the service model: IaaS customers manage more, SaaS customers manage less, but both always manage their own data and access.
details.whyItMatters: Misunderstanding the shared responsibility boundary is the root cause of most cloud security incidents. Clarity about ownership prevents dangerous gaps in protection.
takeaways: Provider responsibility increases from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS
Customers always manage data, access, and configurations
Misunderstanding boundaries leads to security breaches

faq.question: How does shared responsibility change between IaaS and SaaS?
faq.answer: With IaaS, customers manage OS, runtime, applications, and data. With PaaS, the provider also manages the OS and runtime. With SaaS, the provider manages everything except user access, data uploaded, and application configuration settings.

faq.question: Where do most cloud security failures occur?
faq.answer: On the customer side. Misconfigurations, overly permissive access, unencrypted data, and poor identity management are all customer responsibilities. The underlying cloud infrastructure is rarely breached; customer-side errors are the dominant attack vector.
